title: The Fall of Jerusalem
overview: This closing chapter, a historical record nearly identical to the end of 2 Kings, tells how Babylon captured Jerusalem, burned the temple and exiled its people, then ends with a captive king of Judah being released from prison.

parts.label: Zedekiah's reign and revolt (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Zedekiah, Judah's last king, had been placed on the throne by Babylon and broke his sworn loyalty by rebelling against it. The writer sees all that follows as the LORD's judgment on the nation's long wrongdoing, ending with the people pushed out of the land.

parts.label: Siege, escape and capture (vv. 4-11)
parts.note: Babylon's army surrounded Jerusalem for about a year and a half until famine broke the city, and the king fled by night but was caught near Jericho. At Riblah, the Babylonian king's base to the north, Zedekiah was punished as a traitor: his sons were killed before his eyes, then he was blinded and imprisoned for life.

parts.label: The city and temple burned (vv. 12-16)
parts.note: About a month later a Babylonian commander burned the temple, the palace and the great houses, tore down the walls, and took many captive while leaving the poorest to farm. During the exile these dates became fast days, and Jewish tradition still mourns the temple's destruction each year.

parts.label: Temple treasures carried off (vv. 17-23)
parts.note: The huge bronze pillars, the great basin called the Sea and other objects from Solomon's time were smashed for their metal, while gold and silver pieces were taken whole. The careful description of the pillars, drawn from the account of the temple's building, seems meant to show how much beauty was lost.

parts.label: Leaders executed, people counted (vv. 24-30)
parts.note: The chief priest, senior officials and others were taken to Riblah and executed, removing Judah's leadership. The total of 4,600 people across three deportations differs from the numbers in 2 Kings, and scholars are unsure whether it counts only men, certain groups, or separate events.

parts.label: A captive king released (vv. 31-34)
parts.note: In the thirty-seventh year of his exile, Jehoiachin, an earlier king taken in the first deportation, was freed from prison by Nebuchadnezzar's son and given an honored place at the royal table. Many read this quiet ending as a sign that David's royal line survived, and Christians later noted that Jehoiachin appears in the family line leading to Jesus.

disagreement: Readers differ on whether the closing release of Jehoiachin is meant as a deliberate note of hope for the future or simply a sober reminder that Judah's king still lived as a dependent of Babylon.
think: Why might people who lost nearly everything choose to record the exact dates, names and objects of that loss so carefully?
